body_markdown:
As autumn arrives and temperatures begin to fall, many women going through perimenopause or menopause may notice that some symptoms become more difficult to manage. Cooler weather, shorter days, reduced sunlight and changes in daily routines can all influence how the body feels during this stage of life.


Hormonal changes are already responsible for a wide range of menopause symptoms, from hot flushes and disrupted sleep to changes in mood, aches and dry skin. According to women’s health GP and British Menopause Society registered menopause specialist Dr Nikki Ramskill, colder weather can make some of these symptoms feel more challenging for some women.


Here are some of the ways the changing seasons may affect menopause symptoms, along with practical approaches that may help.


## 1. Mood Changes Can Become More Noticeable


Shorter days and reduced exposure to natural light can affect mood and sleep patterns. For someone already experiencing hormonal fluctuations during perimenopause or menopause, these seasonal changes may feel particularly noticeable.


Oestrogen plays a role in brain chemistry, and lower oestrogen levels can affect serotonin and dopamine activity. Reduced daylight can also influence the body's circadian rhythm, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.


Some women may also become more vulnerable to Seasonal Affective Disorder, commonly known as SAD, during periods of reduced daylight.


Getting outside during daylight hours can be a useful part of a healthy daily routine. Even when the weather is cold, spending some time outdoors may provide valuable exposure to natural light while also encouraging movement.


## 2. Cold Weather May Make Aches and Stiffness Feel Worse


Joint and muscle discomfort is another common concern during menopause. Some women report feeling particularly stiff or achy when the weather becomes colder.


Low oestrogen can contribute to aches and pains, while reduced sunlight exposure can affect vitamin D levels. These factors may overlap with lifestyle changes that occur during colder months. When it is dark, wet or cold outside, it can be tempting to spend more time indoors and become less physically active.


Keeping joints warm and maintaining regular movement may help. Gentle walking, stretching, strength exercises or other activities that you enjoy can help you stay active through the colder months.


Some people also report that changes in atmospheric pressure affect joint discomfort. Individual experiences vary, so keeping track of your own symptoms may help you identify whether particular weather conditions appear to affect you.


## 3. Sleep Can Become More Difficult


Sleep problems are already common during menopause, and seasonal changes may add another layer of difficulty.


Less morning sunlight can interfere with the body's natural circadian rhythm. Hormonal changes can also contribute to sleep disruption. Night sweats are a particular issue, and heavy winter clothing or thick bedding can make overheating during the night more uncomfortable.


Creating a consistent bedtime routine can support better sleep. Try to keep your bedroom comfortable rather than excessively warm, and consider breathable nightwear and bedding if night sweats are a problem.


It is also worth paying attention to caffeine intake. During colder weather, people often reach for more tea, coffee or other hot drinks. Increasing caffeine consumption, particularly later in the day, may contribute to sleep difficulties for some people.


## 4. Dry Skin and Irritated Eyes May Become More Noticeable


Menopause can affect the skin because declining oestrogen levels are associated with changes in the skin's natural oils and ceramides. Cold outdoor air, wind and indoor central heating can add to dryness.


As a result, some women may experience increased itching, tightness or general skin discomfort during the colder months. The skin around the eyes can also become dry and irritated. Watery eyes do not always mean the eyes are adequately moisturised. Irritation and dryness can sometimes cause the eyes to water more.


Staying hydrated, protecting exposed skin from cold winds and using suitable moisturising products can be helpful parts of a winter skincare routine.


If eye irritation is persistent or severe, it is sensible to speak with an appropriate healthcare professional.


## 5. Hot Flushes and Feeling Cold Can Happen Together


One of the most frustrating parts of menopause can be experiencing hot flushes while simultaneously feeling cold at other times.


Oestrogen is involved in the body's temperature regulation. During menopause, changes in oestrogen can affect the brain's internal temperature control system. This can contribute to sudden feelings of heat and sweating.


Winter can create an awkward cycle. You may dress in several warm layers because you are cold outside, then enter a centrally heated building and suddenly feel overheated. Removing layers quickly can become necessary when a hot flush starts.


After a flush, some women experience a period of chills or shivering, making the contrast between hot and cold even more uncomfortable.


Layering clothing can therefore be useful because it makes it easier to adjust what you are wearing as your temperature changes.


Alcohol may also make hot flushes worse for some people and can interfere with sleep, so paying attention to individual triggers may be useful during the festive season.


## Simple Ways to Support Yourself Through Winter


There is no single solution that works for everyone experiencing menopause symptoms. Hormone replacement therapy may be appropriate for some women, while others may need alternative approaches depending on their circumstances.


The source article also highlights several lifestyle measures that may support wellbeing during colder months. These include staying hydrated, maintaining regular exercise, spending time outdoors in daylight and following consistent sleep habits. A Mediterranean-style eating pattern, foods containing omega-3 and tryptophan, and appropriate vitamin D intake are also mentioned.


If aches and pains are bothering you, keeping your joints warm and continuing gentle movement may help you remain active. For people affected by reduced winter daylight, light-based approaches such as SAD lamps or glasses are also suggested by the medical expert quoted in the source.


The most important step is to pay attention to your own symptoms. Menopause does not affect every woman in the same way, and seasonal changes may be more noticeable for some people than others.


## When to Speak to a Healthcare Professional


Menopause symptoms can affect everyday life, work, relationships, sleep and emotional wellbeing. You do not necessarily have to simply accept symptoms that are significantly affecting your quality of life.


If symptoms are persistent, severe, changing unexpectedly or difficult to manage, discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional. They can help you understand whether they may be related to menopause and discuss suitable treatment or management options.


It is also important to be cautious about starting supplements or medications based solely on general advice. Individual needs vary, and some treatments or supplements may not be appropriate for everyone.


### Final Thoughts


The arrival of colder weather can bring changes that make menopause symptoms feel more noticeable. Reduced daylight may affect mood and sleep, cold temperatures can make aches and stiffness more uncomfortable, and central heating and winter weather may contribute to dry skin and irritated eyes.


At the same time, menopause-related changes in temperature regulation can make the contrast between cold outdoor conditions and warm indoor environments particularly challenging.


Simple habits such as staying hydrated, keeping active, getting daylight exposure, maintaining good sleep routines and dressing in adaptable layers may make the colder months easier to navigate.


Most importantly, menopause is an individual experience. If symptoms are affecting your everyday life, speaking with a healthcare professional can help you explore appropriate options rather than trying to manage everything alone.


**Disclaimer:** This article is for general information and educational purposes only. It is not intended to provide medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Menopause symptoms and treatment needs vary between individuals. Always speak with a qualified healthcare professional before starting, stopping or changing any medication, supplement or treatment.
